extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating instructional materials, sequences, and curricula using cognitive load theory — i.e., applying human cognitive architecture (working memory/long-term memory) principles to optimize learning. Includes multimedia, worked examples, sequencing, course-level design (4C/ID) and measurement of different load types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human cognitive architecture (working memory & long-term memory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Working memory is capacity- and duration-limited for novel information; long-term memory is effectively unlimited and, once information is stored there, the capacity/duration limits of working memory disappear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction must account for the limited capacity of working memory for novel information and aim to transfer knowledge into organised long-term memory; expertise (information in long-term memory) changes task characteristics for humans and thus affects instructional design implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element interactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Complexity of information (intrinsic cognitive load) is determined by element interactivity: how many interacting elements must be processed simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Element interactivity depends on both the nature of the information and the learner's prior knowledge; instructional measures of complexity must account for learner knowledge. Reducing effective element interactivity (e.g., via worked examples or integration) reduces extraneous load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic cognitive load
rubrics_metrics.description: Load determined by the complexity of the material to be learned (element interactivity) and the learner's expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic load can only be changed by changing what needs to be learned or by changing learner expertise (e.g., sequencing, part-task practice). Designers should recognise when intrinsic load is high and adapt instruction accordingly (e.g., more guided practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraneous cognitive load
rubrics_metrics.description: Load imposed by the way information is presented or by instructional procedures rather than by the material itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraneous load can and should be reduced by better instructional design (e.g., integrate sources to avoid split-attention, avoid redundant/inconsistent information). Most instructional effects arise from variations in extraneous load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Germane cognitive load (redistributive function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Working memory resources devoted to processing intrinsic aspects of the task (i.e., processes productive for learning); current formulation sees germane load as redistributing resources from extraneous to intrinsic processing rather than adding to total load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should both decrease extraneous load and, where appropriate, increase germane processing (e.g., prompting self-explanations), but only if total cognitive load remains within capacity limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise extraneous, optimise germane within capacity limits
rubrics_metrics.description: To promote learning and transfer, cognitive processing irrelevant to learning should be minimised and processing germane to learning optimised, constrained by available cognitive capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should prioritise reducing extraneous demands first; after that, strategies that increase germane processing can be employed if total load stays within working memory limits (e.g., variability to increase germane processing when working memory is not overloaded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Worked example effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying worked examples (full solutions) reduces cognitive load compared to solving conventional problems and facilitates knowledge construction and transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples may be product-oriented, process-oriented, or modelling examples. They are generally more effective for novices and less effective for high-expertise learners (expertise reversal). Good worked examples should avoid split-attention and redundancy; design of effective examples is difficult and may require sequencing and variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal-free effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing conventional problems with goal-free problems (no specific goal state) reduces cognitive load because learners are not forced into means-ends analysis and instead explore problem states and operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal-free tasks can lower extraneous load and focus learners on solutions and state/operator relationships, supporting knowledge construction; useful early in instruction to reduce expensive means-ends processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion problem effect / completion strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Completion problems provide partial solutions that learners must finish; they bridge worked examples and conventional problems and encourage careful study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use completion problems to scaffold learning: start with near-complete solutions and gradually increase the amount learners must generate (guidance fading). Particularly useful in programming and other domains to ensure engagement with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split-attention effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When learners must mentally integrate two or more complementary sources of information (e.g., diagram + separate text), mental integration increases cognitive load and hampers learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent split-attention by physically or temporally integrating information sources; when integration is not possible, consider presenting one source auditorily (modality) or redesigning materials to reduce the need for mental integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting fully redundant sources of information (e.g., diagram + identical text) can impair learning because learners expend effort discovering the redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary duplication of information; present only the most informative source(s) or ensure redundancy actually adds complementary cues rather than duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Working memory can be subdivided into (partially) independent processors (auditory/verbal and visual/pictorial); combining modalities (e.g., diagram + spoken text) can increase effective working memory capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use auditory narration for text that would otherwise induce split-attention with visuals; modality choices should consider transient information effects and learner characteristics. Meta-analytic evidence supports modality benefits under many conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice over variable problem situations tends to encourage construction of generalized knowledge by highlighting invariant features; increases intrinsic load but can increase transfer if total load remains within capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variability to promote transfer when learners are working with low extraneous load (e.g., worked-example learning); avoid high variability when learners already face high total cognitive load (e.g., conventional problem solving without support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise reversal effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional techniques effective for novices (e.g., worked examples, integrated multimedia) can become ineffective or detrimental for more expert learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt instruction to learner expertise: provide more guidance and worked examples to novices; reduce or remove redundant guidance and increase problem solving for experts. Monitor for reversal effects in sequencing and multimedia segmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance-fading effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Gradually reducing instructional support (fading guidance) as learners gain expertise (e.g., moving from worked examples to completion problems to full problems) supports learning and transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement staged fading (completion strategy) so that learners increasingly generate solutions themselves; ensures appropriate allocation of intrinsic/germane/extraneous load across learning phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4C/ID model (four-component instructional design)
rubrics_metrics.description: A course-level instructional design model that designs whole educational programs using four components: (1) learning tasks, (2) supportive information, (3) procedural information/just-in-time (part-task) information, and (4) part-task practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 4C/ID to sequence and integrate complex learning over longer durations (courses/curricula), balancing intrinsic and germane load, and using whole-task practice, supportive information, and part-task automation where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segmentation & temporal coordination (transient information effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal organisation (segmentation) of dynamic multimedia (animation + narration) matters: unsegmented/transient information can overload working memory; segmentation or temporal coordination reduces load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment animations, coordinate narration and visual events, and allow learner-controlled pacing or segmentation to reduce transient information load. Consider segmentation frequency, timing, and expertise interactions (expertise reversal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of cognitive load (multi-method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive load should be measured with a variety of instruments: subjective rating scales (immediate/delayed), physiological measures (pupillary response), dual-task methods, rhythm/behavioral methods, and other objective tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use instruments appropriate to the type of load (intrinsic/extraneous/germane) and research question; repeated measures and method triangulation (subjective + objective) improve validity. Be aware of timing (immediate vs delayed ratings) and the potential to disturb learning when measuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective working-memory / collaborative learning effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaboration can create a collective working memory (multiple brains) that increases effective working memory capacity for complex tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design collaborative tasks to exploit distributed cognition for high element-interactivity tasks, but manage coordination costs and extraneous load introduced by collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain effects alter the characteristics of other, simple cognitive load effects (i.e., compound effects change how other effects manifest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that interventions can interact (e.g., segmentation + expertise effects) and that design changes may alter multiple load dimensions; test for interactions rather than assuming additive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary distinction: biologically primary vs secondary knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate knowledge that humans are evolved to acquire effortlessly (biologically primary) from secondary, culturally-acquired knowledge which requires instruction; this distinction affects instructional design choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect biologically primary skills to be acquired with less direct instruction; secondary knowledge (e.g., formal mathematics) often requires explicit instructional techniques that manage cognitive load (worked examples, sequencing, 4C/ID).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transient information & user interaction considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Transient information (briefly available visual or auditory content) can impose extra load; simple user interactions (e.g., clicks) do not necessarily foster deeper learning and may cause additional processing demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interactive multimedia carefully — ensure interactions reduce rather than add extraneous load; control transient effects via segmentation, pacing, and modality choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaffolding: sequence from examples to problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should scaffold learners: use worked examples and completion problems early, then fade support into conventional problem solving as expertise increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence tasks to manage intrinsic load and to allow accumulation of long-term memory schemas; incorporate variability and increasing complexity once extraneous load is minimised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific knowledge vs generic skill instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain-specific organised knowledge in long-term memory is central to skill; teaching generic skills (e.g., generic problem solving) without domain knowledge is ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus instruction on developing domain-specific schemas and automatized component skills (use part-task practice and worked examples) rather than attempting to teach generic strategies in isolation.
